title: Week 3 review: server troubleshooting
goal: Investigate six classic incidents step by step with real commands: disk full, high CPU, port in use, service will not start, cannot SSH, DNS not resolving.
setup: # S1: a Jenkins home with old workspaces (about 24 MB of real data)
for ws in todo-frontend todo-backend parts-service old-job-2024 experiment-ml; do mkdir -p "jenkins-home/workspace/$ws"; done
# S2: a report job that got stuck in a busy loop
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# nightly report (stuck in a loop by mistake)' 'while :; do :; done' > report-generator.sh
# S4: a service that checks its config before it starts

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# todo-svc: read todo.conf, check it, then serve www/ on PORT' 'cd "$(dirname "$0")"' 'source ./todo.conf' 'log() { echo "$(date +%F) $*" >> logs/todo-svc.log; }' 'if ! [[ $PORT =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then log "FATAL invalid PORT value: $PORT"; exit 3; fi' 'if [ -z "$DB_URL" ]; then log "FATAL DB_URL is not set"; exit 3; fi' 'log "INFO starting on port $PORT"' 'exec python3 -m http.server "$PORT" --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory www' > svc/todo-svc.sh
# S5: a key copied from Windows with loose permissions

warmup.q: How do you list the contents of `app.tar.gz` without extracting?
`df` shows a full disk, `du` shows little. What do you check?
warmup.a: Deleted files that a process still holds open: `sudo lsof +L1`.

warmup.q: How do you find the process that listens on port 8080?

warmup.a: Wrong key, wrong user, or bad permissions on `~/.ssh` / the key / `authorized_keys`.

problems.title: Scenario 1: disk full on the Jenkins server
problems.situation: Jenkins builds fail with `No space left on device`. The `workspace` folder under `jenkins-home` is the usual suspect. Find what is big and old, and clean it safely with a dry run first.
task: Show the total size of `jenkins-home/workspace` and each workspace, biggest last.
List workspaces not changed for more than 30 days.
Dry run: print the old workspaces that would be deleted.
Delete them, and show the new total.
hints: Same find with `-print` first, then `-exec rm -rf {} +`.
solution: echo "=== not changed for 30+ days (dry run) ==="

explanation.meaning: On a real server, first find the full filesystem (`df -h`, `df -i`).
Walk down to the biggest folders (Day 17).
Only the workspace folders themselves, not files inside them.
Not changed for more than 30 days (Day 12).
Dry run, then the same test with the action.
Jenkins "Discard old builds" and workspace cleanup in the pipeline, plus a disk alert (Day 17 P5).

problems.expected_output:
25M	jenkins-home/workspace
1.1M	jenkins-home/workspace/parts-service
2.1M	jenkins-home/workspace/todo-frontend
3.1M	jenkins-home/workspace/todo-backend
8.1M	jenkins-home/workspace/old-job-2024
11M	jenkins-home/workspace/experiment-ml
=== not changed for 30+ days (dry run) ===
jenkins-home/workspace/experiment-ml
jenkins-home/workspace/old-job-2024
=== after cleanup ===
6.1M	jenkins-home/workspace
mistakes: `rm -rf jenkins-home/workspace/*` deletes the workspaces of running builds too.
Cleaning without finding the cause: the disk fills again tomorrow. Add build retention and monitoring.
problems.interview_say: I find the full filesystem with `df -h`, walk down with `du -sh | sort -h`, list old data with `find -mtime`, dry-run, then delete. Then I fix the cause: retention settings and a disk alert.
problems.try_yourself: Compress instead of delete: `tar -czf old-job.tgz -C jenkins-home/workspace old-job-2024` (run Reset and setup again first).

problems.title: Scenario 2: high CPU on the training server
problems.situation: The model training server is slow and the fans are loud. Find which process uses the CPU, check what it is, try a lower priority, and stop it if it is a mistake.
task: Start the problem: `bash report-generator.sh &` (it is a stuck loop).
Check the load and CPU count (`uptime`, `nproc`).
Show the top CPU processes with `ps -eo pid,pcpu,args --sort=-pcpu | head`.
Check what the top process is (`/proc/PID/cmdline`, `ps -o lstart=`). Lower its priority with `renice`.
It is a stuck job: stop it with SIGTERM and check it is gone.
hints: In `top`, press `P` to sort by CPU.
`renice -n 19 -p PID` = lowest priority (allowed for the user's own processes).

explanation.meaning: Load compared with CPU count: is the machine really overloaded? (Day 17)
Biggest CPU users first (Day 15).
Exactly what was started (Day 15).
If the job is needed but not urgent, make it nice instead of killing it.
If it is a mistake, stop it cleanly; `kill -9` only if needed.
High `wa` in `vmstat` = waiting for disk; high `si/so` = swapping (memory). Then CPU is not the real problem.

problems.expected_output:
load: 0.14 0.07 0.01, CPUs: 4
  PID %CPU COMMAND
29093 99.0 bash report-generator.sh
top process: bash report-generator.sh
niceness now:  19
stuck job stopped
problems.output_note: PIDs, load and %CPU values are different on every run.
mistakes: Killing the top CPU process without checking what it is. It can be the database doing important work.
Looking only at CPU. A slow server can also be swapping or waiting for disk: check `free -m` and `vmstat 1 5` too.
problems.interview_say: For high CPU I check load against `nproc`, find the process with `top` or `ps --sort=-pcpu`, find out what it is, then renice, fix or stop it. I also check memory and I/O wait, because they can look like a CPU problem.
problems.try_yourself: Run `top -b -n 1 | head -n 15` while the loop runs (start it again). Find the line for `bash`.

problems.title: Scenario 3: port in use after a failed pipeline
problems.situation: On the CI machine, the integration test starts the app on port 8095 and fails with `Address already in use`. The last pipeline crashed and left its test server running. Find it with `ss`, confirm it, stop it, and rerun.
task: Simulate the leftover: start a test server on 8095 in the background.
Start the "new" one on 8095 and save its error in `start.log`. Show the last line.
Find the owner with `ss -ltnp 'sport = :8095'`. Print only the program name and check the full command with `ps`.
Stop it with `fuser -k -TERM 8095/tcp`, start the new server, and test it with curl.
hints: `grep -o 'pid=[0-9]*'` and `cut -d= -f2` get the PID from that text.
`fuser -k -TERM 8095/tcp` sends SIGTERM to every process using that port.
solution: python3 -m http.server 8095 --bind 127.0.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &    # leftover from the crashed pipeline

explanation.meaning: `Address already in use` names the problem exactly.
Find the listener and its PID (Day 18). Use sudo for other users' processes.
Confirm it is really the old test server, not a real service.
Send SIGTERM to the port owner. Another tool for the same job as `lsof -t` + `kill`.
Pipelines should stop test servers in a `post { always { ... } }` block or with `trap` (Day 22), or use random free ports.

problems.expected_output:
OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use
program: python3
command: python3 -m http.server 8095 --bind 127.0.0.1
new test server: 200
mistakes: Using a fixed port for tests on a shared CI agent: two pipelines at the same time will clash.
problems.interview_say: I read the error, find the listener with `ss -ltnp`, confirm the process with `ps`, stop it cleanly, and then fix the pipeline so it always cleans up its test servers.
problems.try_yourself: Find a free port with Python: `python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("",0)); print(s.getsockname()[1])'`.

problems.title: Scenario 4: the service will not start (find the config bugs)
problems.situation: After a config change, `todo-svc` exits right after start. With systemd the user would run `systemctl status` and `journalctl -u`. Here the service writes its own log. Read the exit code and the log, compare the config with the example, fix it, and start again.
task: Start it: `bash todo-svc.sh`. Print the exit code.
Read the last line of `logs/todo-svc.log`.
Compare `todo.conf` with `todo.conf.example` using `diff`.
Fix the config (`sed -i` for PORT, add the missing DB_URL). Start the service in the background and test `/health.json`.
hints: The exit code (3) and the FATAL line say exactly what is wrong.
solution: bash todo-svc.sh; echo "exit code: $?"             # it fails again: a second problem
bash todo-svc.sh > /dev/null 2>&1 &                # now it starts and keeps running

explanation.meaning: The service reports that it failed on purpose (config check).
Last log line without the date column. With systemd: `journalctl -u todo-svc -n 20`.
Compare with a known good config to see wrong and missing lines (Day 2).
Fix the value, append the missing line (Day 11, Day 4).
`systemctl status todo-svc` → `journalctl -u todo-svc -n 50` → fix → `systemctl restart todo-svc`.

problems.expected_output:
exit code: 3
FATAL invalid PORT value: eighty
1c1,2
< PORT=eighty
---
> PORT=8097
> DB_URL=postgres://db.todo.local:5432/todo
exit code: 3
FATAL DB_URL is not set
{"status":"UP"}
INFO starting on port 8097
mistakes: Restarting the service again and again without reading the log. The log says why.
Fixing only the first error. Run again after each fix: here a second problem (DB_URL) appears after PORT is fixed.
problems.interview_say: When a service does not start, I check `systemctl status` and `journalctl -u name` for the real error, compare the config with a known good one, fix one thing at a time, and restart.
problems.try_yourself: Add `TIMEOUT=abc` to the config and a check for it in `todo-svc.sh` (number only). Test it.

problems.title: Scenario 5: cannot SSH to the server
problems.situation: A teammate says "SSH to prod does not work". Instead of guessing, the user writes a small check script that tests, in order: the name, the port, and the key file permissions. Here it runs against a local port where no SSH server listens.
task: Write `ssh-check.sh HOST PORT KEY` with three checks: name resolves (`getent hosts`), port open (`nc -z -w 2`), key is 600 (`stat -c %a`).
Print OK or a clear FAIL message for each check, with a hint.
Run it for `localhost 2222 keys/prod_key`.
Fix the key permission and run it again. What is left?
hints: `nc -z -w 2 "$HOST" "$PORT"` exits 0 when the port is open.
solution: if getent hosts "$HOST" > /dev/null; then echo "OK   name $HOST resolves"
else echo "FAIL name $HOST does not resolve -> check DNS, /etc/hosts, typo"; fi
if nc -z -w 2 "$HOST" "$PORT" 2>/dev/null; then echo "OK   port $PORT is open"
else echo "FAIL port $PORT is closed or filtered -> sshd running? security group? right port?"; fi
if [ "$PERM" = 600 ] || [ "$PERM" = 400 ]; then echo "OK   key $KEY has permission $PERM"
else echo "FAIL key $KEY has permission $PERM -> chmod 600 $KEY"; fi

explanation.meaning: Name → network/port → authentication. Each layer needs the one before it.
Name resolution (Day 18).
TCP port test with a 2 second timeout. Refused = nothing listens; timeout = firewall.
Key permissions (Day 19): SSH ignores keys that others can read.
Here no sshd runs on 2222. On a real server: `systemctl status ssh`, `ss -ltn | grep :22`, the security group, or the cloud console.
If all three are OK and it still fails: `ssh -v` and the server log (`journalctl -u ssh`, `/var/log/auth.log`).

problems.expected_output:
OK   name localhost resolves
FAIL port 2222 is closed or filtered -> sshd running? security group? right port?
FAIL key keys/prod_key has permission 644 -> chmod 600 keys/prod_key
--- after chmod ---
OK   name localhost resolves
FAIL port 2222 is closed or filtered -> sshd running? security group? right port?
OK   key keys/prod_key has permission 600
mistakes: Jumping to `ssh -vvv` first. Simple checks (name, port, key) find most problems faster.
Opening port 22 to `0.0.0.0/0` in the security group to "fix" it. Allow only the team's IP addresses, or use a bastion or SSM.
problems.interview_say: For SSH problems I check in layers: does the name resolve, is port 22 reachable, then the key, user and permissions. After that, `ssh -v` and the server's auth log show the exact reason.
problems.try_yourself: Add a fourth check: the user name, using `ssh -G "$HOST" | awk '/^user /{print $2}'`.

problems.title: Scenario 6: DNS not resolving — is it DNS or the app?
problems.situation: The frontend cannot reach `http://todo.internal:8096`. The app team says "our app is up". The user proves where the problem is: first the name, then the app itself, by pointing the name at the right IP for one curl request only (no system change).
task: Start the "app" on 127.0.0.1:8096 (a test server).
Try `curl` with the name. Print the exit code.
Check the name with `getent hosts todo.internal`.
Test the app with the name, but give curl the IP yourself: `curl --resolve todo.internal:8096:127.0.0.1 ...`.
Write down the conclusion and the real fix.
hints: curl exit code 6 = could not resolve host.
`--resolve HOST:PORT:IP` makes curl use that IP for that name and port. Nothing on the system changes.
If it works with `--resolve`, the app is fine and DNS (or /etc/hosts) is the problem.
solution: curl -s --max-time 5 http://todo.internal:8096/health.json; echo "curl by name: exit code $?"
getent hosts todo.internal || echo "getent: no answer for todo.internal (exit code $?)"
echo "conclusion: the app answers; the name does not resolve -> fix DNS"

explanation.meaning: curl could not resolve the host name: no IP, so no connection was even tried.
Same resolver as programs: hosts file + DNS (Day 18).
Bypass DNS for one request. Proves the app works.
Create or fix the DNS record (for example in Route 53 or CoreDNS), check the `search` domain in `/etc/resolv.conf`, or in Kubernetes use the service name `todo-backend.default.svc.cluster.local`.
`dig todo.internal` and `dig @10.0.0.2 todo.internal` show what each DNS server answers.

problems.expected_output:
curl by name: exit code 6
getent: no answer for todo.internal (exit code 2)
{"status":"UP"}
conclusion: the app answers; the name does not resolve -> fix DNS
mistakes: Adding the name to `/etc/hosts` on every server as the "fix". It hides the DNS problem and breaks when the IP changes.
Testing with `ping`: if ICMP is blocked, DNS problems and network problems look the same.
problems.interview_say: To separate DNS from app problems, I check `getent hosts name` or `dig`, then call the app by IP or with `curl --resolve`. If the app answers by IP, I fix DNS, not the app.
problems.try_yourself: Run `curl -sv --resolve todo.internal:8096:127.0.0.1 http://todo.internal:8096/ 2>&1 | grep -i 'added\|connected'` while the server runs.

interview.q: Scenario: "The server is slow." What do you check first?
interview.a: `uptime` (load vs `nproc`), `top` (CPU and memory per process), `free -m` (available, swap), `vmstat 1 5` (wa = disk wait, si/so = swap), `df -h` (full disk), then the app logs.

interview.q: Scenario: "No space left on device." What do you do?
interview.a: `df -h` and `df -i` to find the filesystem, `du -xh --max-depth=1 | sort -h` to find big folders, `lsof +L1` for deleted-open files, clean safely, then fix retention and add alerts.

interview.q: Scenario: "The app does not start: port already in use."
interview.a: `ss -ltnp | grep :PORT` or `lsof -i :PORT` to find the process, check it with `ps`, stop it cleanly, start the app, and fix whatever left the old process running.

interview.q: Scenario: "The service fails to start after a deploy."
interview.a: `systemctl status name`, `journalctl -u name -n 50`, check the config (compare with the last good one or `git diff`), `systemd-analyze verify` for unit changes, fix one thing, restart.

interview.q: Scenario: "I cannot SSH to the server."
interview.a: Check the name (`getent hosts`), the port (`nc -zv host 22`; refused vs timeout), the security group, then the key, user and permissions, and `ssh -v`. On the server: `journalctl -u ssh` or `/var/log/auth.log`.
`getent hosts` / `dig` for DNS, then curl by IP or `curl --resolve` to test the app, `nc -zv` for the port. If only the name fails, fix DNS or the search domain.
